transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess what brought me in is that I just can't keep my mind on one thing anymore. Like, I'll be right in the middle of fixing a rendering bug at work—which, honestly, the whole engine we're using is a complete mess right now because the original guy just hardcoded all the lighting variables, but anyway—I'll be fixing it, and then a Slack ping goes off, or I notice this color pattern on my second monitor, or even a siren goes by outside. And suddenly I'm pulled into a whole new idea before I even finish the line of code. 

Speaking of sirens, they've been going past my apartment constantly this week. I live over near the avenue where they're doing all that construction, tearing up the water mains, and the smell of the wet dirt and tar is just... it gets into the vents, you know? Did you have to drive through that to get to the clinic today? Because the traffic is just unbelievable right now. But yeah, I just... my mind just keeps jumping away from the code like that.
Are these distractions and jumps in your attention causing you any significant problems or stress at work or in your daily life?

Well, yeah, I guess you could say it's causing problems. My employer actually just put me on administrative leave. I got so frustrated waiting for the approvals—because our QA team takes literally three days to run basic regression tests, which is completely insane when we're supposed to be in a two-week agile sprint. I remember back at my first job right after I got my degree, we deployed every Friday, no red tape, just straight to the servers. So anyway, I just bypassed the whole approval queue and deployed the changes to production on my own. Because I knew the code was right! But management freaked out and sent me home. 

And then at home... well, my wife says things feel really unstable right now. We've been arguing a lot, mostly about my spending. But honestly, I just bought some necessary upgrades for my home office since I'm here so much now. I ordered this custom split ergonomic keyboard from Germany, the one with the Cherry MX brown switches, because the tactile bump is just so much better for my typing speed. I actually had to order three of them to test the different spring weights, and the shipping was a total nightmare. It got held up in customs in Chicago for like a week and a half, and the tracking number just stopped updating. Have you ever had a package get stuck in Chicago? It's like a black hole for international mail. But yeah, she's really upset about the money and the arguments, so it's pretty stressful all around.
Did you feel like you thought through the potential consequences before deploying the changes to production on your own?

Well, I mean, I thought through the consequences of *not* doing it. If I waited for another review cycle, it felt like letting the whole opportunity die. The timing was critical, you know? But I guess I didn't think about the HR side of it. I just pushed the update without approval because it had to be done. 

Just like with the side project I'm launching. I spent money we hadn't agreed on for all these GPUs, print materials, and promo videos. Which, honestly, the video production company I hired was completely incompetent. They kept getting the lighting wrong on the green screen, and I had to step in and show them how to adjust the key light because they were washing out the whole background. I used to do a lot of photography in college—mostly black and white film, developing it myself in the darkroom. The smell of the chemicals, the stop bath, it's so distinct. Have you ever developed your own film? It's a dying art, really. Everyone just uses their phones now, but the dynamic range on a real silver gelatin print is just unmatched. But yeah, my wife was furious about the money for the GPUs and the videos. She doesn't see the vision yet.
Did you feel like you were acting on impulse when you decided to deploy the changes to production without approval?

Yeah, I guess you could call it an impulse, but in the moment, it just felt like clarity, you know? Like I said, I pushed that update without approval because waiting for another review cycle felt like letting the whole opportunity die. It was just so obvious what needed to happen. Just like with the side project. I spent money we hadn't agreed on for all those GPUs, the print materials, and the promo videos because the timing was perfect. 

Speaking of timing, I actually had to time the delivery of the GPUs perfectly because the delivery guys always leave the boxes right on the front porch where anyone can see them. I live on a corner lot, and the foot traffic is just ridiculous. Mostly people walking their dogs. There's this one guy with a golden retriever that just refuses to walk on the sidewalk—always in the grass, always sniffing the same fire hydrant. I read somewhere that dogs have like 300 million olfactory receptors in their noses compared to our six million. It's crazy to think about how they experience the world, just this constant stream of smells. Do you have a dog? I've always wanted a husky, but the shedding would probably destroy the fans on my new GPUs. But yeah, I just... I acted on what needed to be done, even if my wife thinks it was impulsive.
Do you think your actions and decisions have caused problems in your relationship with your wife?

Yeah, I mean... absolutely. It's definitely causing problems. Like I said before, my wife says things feel really unstable right now. We've been arguing constantly about the spending for the GPUs and the promo materials. And it's not just at home, it's work too. I mean, my employer put me on administrative leave after I bypassed the approval queue and deployed those changes on my own. 

Which, honestly, being on leave has given me so much time to look into day trading. I started watching these tutorials on candlestick patterns and Fibonacci retracements. It's fascinating how the market moves in these predictable waves if you know what to look for. I actually started tracking the historical data of this one obscure altcoin, and the chart patterns are almost identical to the dot-com bubble in the late 90s. Did you invest in tech stocks back then? I remember my uncle lost his shirt on Pets.com. He had this whole basement full of those little sock puppet mascots. He ended up giving them out at Halloween instead of candy for like three years straight. Can you imagine being a kid and getting a corporate mascot puppet instead of a Snickers? But yeah... my wife is really upset about the arguments and the instability, so I guess you could say it's causing problems.
Do you feel like your impulsive decisions are affecting your ability to function effectively in your daily life or relationships?

Well, yeah, I guess you could say it's affecting things. I mean, like I was saying, my employer put me on administrative leave because I bypassed the approval queue and deployed those changes on my own. And at home, my wife is just... she says the spending on the GPUs and all our arguments have made things feel really unstable. 

Speaking of unstable, you should see the foundation on my house. We had a guy come out to look at this crack in the drywall, and he ended up going under the crawlspace and finding all this water damage. Apparently, the grading in the backyard is completely wrong, so every time it rains, the water just pools right against the concrete. I started looking into French drains—did you know you can actually dig them yourself if you rent a trencher? I was watching these videos of guys just tearing up their yards with these massive machines. It looks incredibly satisfying, just ripping through the dirt and roots. I almost rented one from Home Depot last weekend, but the guy at the counter said you have to call 811 first to mark the utility lines. Which makes sense, I guess. You don't want to hit a gas main. Have you ever done any landscaping like that? It's crazy how much work goes into just moving water away from a house. But yeah, my wife is definitely not happy with how things are going, and work is... well, it's on pause right now.
Have you always felt like you act on impulses, or is this something that has changed for you over time?

No, it's definitely not how I usually am. I mean, I've always been driven, but this... this specific way of just knowing what to do and acting on it instantly? That's new. It started about three months ago, right around the time my platform was selected for the Glendale showcase. 

Which was a huge deal, by the way. Glendale is like the premier tech convention for our sector. They have it at this massive convention center that used to be an old airplane hangar. The architecture is incredible—all these exposed steel beams and massive skylights. I was reading about how they retrofitted the HVAC system to handle the heat load of all those servers and displays. They actually use a geothermal cooling loop that goes down like 400 feet into the bedrock. It's brilliant, really. Using the earth's natural temperature to chill the water before it cycles back up. I thought about trying to build a miniature version of that for my GPU rig at home. You just need a deep enough hole and some copper tubing. I even started pricing out augers on Craigslist. You'd be surprised how many people buy heavy machinery for one project and then just want to get rid of it. Have you ever been to Glendale? The food trucks they get for that event are insane. There was this one truck selling fusion tacos—Korean BBQ beef with kimchi slaw in a handmade corn tortilla. I think I ate there three days in a row. But yeah, this whole impulsive thing, it really just kicked into high gear about three months ago when the Glendale thing happened.
Have you been feeling more energetic than usual over the past three months?

Yeah, energetic doesn't even begin to cover it. I've been running on this constant current, you know? Like, I wake up and I'm already planning out new features, the exhibition layouts for Glendale, all the press angles, and the code changes. Sitting still just feels like... like I'm wasting the moment. There's just so much to do. 

Speaking of doing things, I actually started looking into how they manufacture those press lanyards. You know the ones with the little plastic clips? It turns out the injection molding process for those is fascinating. They use these massive hoppers of plastic pellets, melt them down, and force them into these steel molds under incredible pressure. I was watching this documentary on how they make the molds themselves—they use CNC machines that can cut steel with microscopic precision. I started thinking, why buy promo materials when I could just buy a small desktop CNC machine and make my own custom metal badges? I found this guy on a forum who built one out of old printer parts and stepper motors. It's amazing what you can do with a little ingenuity and some open-source software. I actually spent like six hours last night mapping out the schematics for it. Have you ever tried 3D printing or CNC machining? It's like having a tiny factory right on your desk. But yeah, to answer your question, the energy has been off the charts. I just can't stop moving.
Have you been having trouble sleeping or noticed any changes in your sleep pattern over the past three months?

Trouble sleeping? I'm not really sure, I haven't really paid attention to it. I guess I just sleep when I sleep, I haven't noticed any real trouble. 

My wife actually got one of those smart rings a while back that tracks your REM cycles and all that. The technology packed into those tiny things is unbelievable. They use these optical sensors—photoplethysmography, I think it's called—to measure your blood volume changes using green and red LED lights. I ended up taking apart an old smartwatch last month just to see how the sensor array was actually soldered to the logic board. The micro-soldering is so precise, you need a digital microscope just to see the pins. 

I actually bought a soldering station with a hot air rework gun because I figured I could start repairing my own electronics instead of throwing them out. E-waste is a massive problem globally, you know? Millions of tons of lithium-ion batteries and rare earth metals just sitting in landfills. You can actually extract pure gold from old CPU pins if you use a mix of nitric and hydrochloric acid. It's called aqua regia. I watched a guy do it online, and he got like a solid gram of gold out of a bucket of old Pentium processors. I seriously thought about trying it in the garage, but you need a proper fume hood for the toxic gas, and the ventilation setup would take a few days to build. Have you ever melted metal down? It's fascinating watching it change states. 

But yeah, as far as my sleep goes... I haven't really noticed anything different.
Have you been sleeping less than usual over the past three months?

Sleeping less? I mean, maybe? I don't really track the hours. I just kind of go until I don't need to, so I couldn't tell you if it's actually less time. 

I don't really look at the clock much these days anyway. Clocks are actually a really weird concept if you think about it. The way we measure time is so arbitrary for humans, but for computers, time synchronization is a massive, massive headache. You have to use NTP—Network Time Protocol—just to keep servers from drifting. Even a few milliseconds of drift can completely corrupt a distributed database. They actually use atomic clocks for the really critical stuff, measuring the vibration of cesium atoms. I was reading this white paper on how they're developing optical lattice clocks that use strontium now, and they're so precise they won't lose a single second in like 15 billion years. It's wild. 

I was actually thinking about writing a custom script to sync all my home devices directly to a stratum 1 time server just to see if I could eliminate local network latency entirely. Have you ever noticed how your microwave clock is always like a minute or two off from your phone? It drives me completely crazy. I actually took the microwave apart on Tuesday to see if I could wire a tiny Wi-Fi module into the control board to force it to auto-sync with an NTP server. You just have to bypass the main relay and tap into the 5-volt rail, but the schematics are all in Korean, so I had to use this machine learning translation tool to decipher the wiring diagram. 

But yeah, as for sleeping less... I just haven't really been counting the hours. I'm not sure.
Have you been feeling unusually happy or euphoric when you act on these impulses?

Yeah, euphoric is... I mean, lit up. That's how I'd describe it. Most days I feel completely lit up and unstoppable, like the whole Glendale project finally caught up with what I've been building in my head. It's an incredible rush. But then my wife or the guys at work try to slow me down, talking about "process" and "code review," and I just snap. I snap hard. It's like they're driving in the slow lane while I'm in a Formula 1 car. 

Speaking of Formula 1, the aerodynamics on those cars are absolutely insane. They use computational fluid dynamics to model the airflow over the front wing, and they can tweak the downforce by millimeter adjustments. I was looking at the telemetry data from last season—someone dumped a massive CSV file on GitHub—and I started writing a Python script to visualize the tire degradation curves based on track temperature. It’s crazy how the rubber compounds blister when they hit 120 degrees Celsius. I actually started looking into buying some raw synthetic rubber just to see how it vulcanizes. You need sulfur and extreme heat to create the cross-links between the polymer chains. I figured I could probably build a small vulcanization oven in the backyard using some firebricks and a propane burner. You can get firebricks really cheap from old pottery kilns. Have you ever tried throwing pottery? The centrifugal force of the wheel is actually a really elegant physics problem. 

But yeah, when people get in my way and don't see the vision, I get really, really irritable. I just don't have time for their speed bumps when I'm feeling this good.
Have you experienced any periods of abnormally elevated or irritable mood that lasted for several days or more?

Yeah, definitely for several days. I mean, it's been most days lately where I just feel completely lit up. Unstoppable. Like the whole Glendale project finally caught up with what I've been building in my head for months. It's just this constant, humming energy. But then, you know, I get these moments where I just snap. Like, I snap hard. My wife or the guys at work, they try to slow me down, talking about "process" and "code review," and it just infuriates me. 

It's like... speaking of code review, the whole concept of version control is actually fascinating. Git was created by Linus Torvalds in like two weeks because he hated the proprietary system they were using for the Linux kernel. The way it uses a directed acyclic graph to track commits is brilliant. I actually started mapping out a completely new version control architecture last weekend. I realized that if you use a blockchain-style immutable ledger, you could decentralize the entire repository structure without relying on a central server like GitHub. I bought three Raspberry Pis to set up a local cluster just to test the consensus algorithm I wrote. I had to custom-compile the OS to strip out all the unnecessary background processes to maximize the CPU cycles. You wouldn't believe how much bloatware is in standard Linux distributions these days. 

I was reading about how they use lightweight containers in enterprise edge computing, and I figured I could containerize my entire home network. I started writing Dockerfiles for my smart thermostat and the garage door opener. The garage door opener uses a rolling code system for security, which is actually a really elegant cryptographic solution. It uses a pseudorandom number generator, so the signal changes every time you press the button. I bought a software-defined radio—an RTL-SDR dongle—just to intercept the 315 megahertz signal and see if I could reverse-engineer the seed value. It's totally legal as long as it's your own equipment, you know? 

But yeah, the mood thing... it's been going on for days, maybe weeks. I feel incredible until someone tries to put the brakes on me, and then I just lose it.
Do you ever have days where you don't feel lit up or unstoppable?

Days where I don't... no. Not lately. It's been pretty constant for about three months now, ever since my platform was selected for the Glendale showcase. It's just been this non-stop drive. 

Speaking of the showcase, the logistics for an event that size are actually totally fascinating. I looked into the ticketing system they're using, and they're relying on these legacy standard QR codes. Which, okay, the math behind QR codes is actually brilliant. It uses Reed-Solomon error correction, so you can literally deface like thirty percent of the image and the scanner can still reconstruct the entire data payload. It's polynomial mathematics at its finest. But it's completely static and vulnerable to cloning. 

I actually stayed up for a couple of nights last week prototyping a dynamic, time-based matrix code instead. It uses a rolling hash function, kind of like a two-factor authenticator but visually encoded. I had to buy a commercial-grade laser scanner off eBay just to test the read-latency. Lasers are amazing if you really think about the physics of them. Stimulated emission of radiation. I was reading a paper on how they use laser interferometry at LIGO to detect gravitational waves from colliding black holes. They're measuring spatial distortions smaller than a single proton across four kilometers of vacuum tubing! It's mind-blowing. 

I actually ordered some first-surface mirrors and a beam splitter because I figured I could build a miniature Michelson interferometer in the basement to measure micro-seismic activity in the neighborhood. You just have to isolate the optical table from the HVAC vibrations. I'm thinking I can build a magnetic levitation platform using some neodymium magnets and a custom PID controller to keep it perfectly level. I just need to wind my own copper electromagnets to get the tuning right... but anyway, what were you asking about? The showcase?
Have you ever had a period of time where you felt extremely happy, irritable, or energetic for several days or more, and acted impulsively during that time?

Impulsive? I mean... I guess some people are calling it that. My wife was pretty upset because I spent money we hadn't agreed on. I bought a cluster of high-end GPUs, ordered all these premium print materials, and commissioned a bunch of promo videos for the showcase. And at work, I just went ahead and pushed a massive update to the main branch without getting approval. I had to, though! Waiting for another of their endless review cycles felt like letting the whole opportunity just die on the vine. You can't pause innovation for bureaucracy. 

Speaking of the GPUs, though, the parallel processing architecture on the new cards is absolutely unbelievable. They use these dedicated Tensor Cores that are specifically optimized for deep learning matrix multiplications. I started reading through the raw CUDA documentation last night because I realized I could write a custom script to bypass the CPU bottleneck and offload the video rendering directly into the VRAM. 

It actually got me looking into how they manufacture the silicon wafers. Did you know the fabrication process requires a cleanroom that is literally ten thousand times cleaner than a hospital operating room? They use extreme ultraviolet lithography now. It's basically shooting a microscopic laser at a microscopic droplet of molten tin to create a plasma that emits the exact wavelength of light they need. I was thinking about it, and I actually started looking up how to build a rudimentary vacuum chamber in the garage to see if I could do some basic plasma etching on my own. You really just need a two-stage rotary vane pump, which you can usually find pretty cheap from old HVAC repair guys on Craigslist. 

My air conditioner actually broke last summer and I took the entire compressor apart before the technician got there. The way the refrigerant undergoes phase changes to absorb and release heat is a beautiful application of thermodynamics. I ended up buying a manifold gauge set... wait, what were we talking about? The showcase promo videos?
Do you feel like your impulsive actions are causing you significant distress or problems in your life?

Distress? I mean, it's definitely causing some friction. My wife is really upset about the spending, and she keeps saying things feel unstable at home because of the arguments. And work... well, they actually put me on administrative leave after I pushed that code without approval. They called it a "breach of protocol," which is just ridiculous. 

But you know, being on leave has actually given me so much time to focus on the home network containerization project. I was looking at the router logs yesterday, and the amount of background noise on the 2.4 gigahertz band is insane. Everyone's microwaves and Bluetooth devices are just polluting the spectrum. Bluetooth itself is fascinating, though—it was named after a tenth-century Viking king, Harald Bluetooth, because he united the Danish tribes, and the technology was meant to unite communication protocols. The frequency-hopping spread spectrum it uses is actually based on a patent co-invented by Hedy Lamarr during World War II to prevent torpedoes from being jammed. She was a Hollywood actress, but also this brilliant inventor. 

It makes you think about how many people have these hidden talents that just get suppressed by their environment. Like, if you don't have the right tools, you can't build the things in your head. That's why I started looking into buying a 3D printer last night—a resin one, not the standard FDM type, because the layer resolution on stereolithography is just vastly superior. You use ultraviolet light to cure liquid photopolymer resin layer by layer. I figured if I can print my own custom enclosures for the Raspberry Pi cluster, I won't have to rely on cheap plastic cases that don't dissipate heat properly. Heat dissipation is the real enemy of processing power. If you don't manage the thermal load, the CPU throttles itself and you lose all that efficiency. I was actually drawing up plans for a custom water-cooling loop using miniature aquarium pumps... wait, what were you asking? About my wife?
Do you think your impulsive actions are damaging your relationship with your wife?

Damaging? I mean, she says things feel really unstable right now because of all the arguments about the money I spent. And with my job putting me on administrative leave for deploying that code without approval, she's definitely stressed about our income. But honestly, the leave is a blessing in disguise because it frees me up for the showcase and my other projects. 

Like the water-cooling loop I was talking about! I actually realized that standard distilled water isn't the best coolant because it can still cause galvanic corrosion if you mix metals in the loop, like copper blocks with aluminum radiators. You need a biocide and a corrosion inhibitor, or better yet, a specialized dielectric fluid. Dielectric fluids are incredible—they don't conduct electricity at all, so you could literally submerge the entire motherboard in a tank of it and it would run perfectly. They use two-phase immersion cooling in massive enterprise data centers now. The fluid boils right on the hot components, turns into vapor, rises to a condenser coil, and drips back down. It's the most efficient heat transfer mechanism possible because it leverages the latent heat of vaporization. 

I was actually pricing out a small glass aquarium and some fluorochemical fluids online this morning. The fluid is expensive, but if I seal the tank perfectly, there's zero loss. I'd just need to design a custom lid with airtight cable glands for the I/O ports. I was thinking I could use a two-part marine epoxy to seal the gaps. Marine epoxy is fascinating stuff—it cures through a chemical exothermic reaction rather than drying, so it can harden completely underwater. They use it to repair the hulls of submarines and deep-sea submersibles. The pressure down in the Mariana Trench is over a thousand times standard atmospheric pressure at sea level. It's over sixteen thousand pounds per square inch! It's amazing that human engineering can withstand that kind of crushing force. 

I was watching this documentary on the Trieste bathyscaphe, the first vessel to reach the bottom of the trench in 1960. They used a massive float filled with gasoline because gasoline is lighter than water and incompressible. It's such a simple, elegant solution to buoyancy control... wait, what did you ask me? About my wife being stressed?
Have you ever had a period where you felt extremely happy, energetic, and impulsive that lasted for several days or more?

Happy and energetic? Yeah, absolutely. Most days lately I feel completely lit up and just... unstoppable. It’s like Glendale finally caught up with what I’ve been building all this time. But I will admit, I snap pretty hard when my wife or my coworkers try to slow me down with what they call "process." 

Process! Don't even get me started on process. At work, they are obsessed with Agile methodologies, and we use Jira to track every little thing. Jira is such a bloated piece of software now. Did you know it was originally built just for bug tracking, and the name actually comes from "Gojira", which is the Japanese name for Godzilla? They named it that because it was supposed to be a competitor to Bugzilla, which was this old Mozilla project back in the late 90s. 

The internet back then was so much more raw and decentralized. You had to dial in with those 56k modems, and that crazy screeching handshake sound you'd hear? That was actually the modems negotiating the connection speed and protocol. It's a process called "training", where they send test signals back and forth to measure the signal-to-noise ratio on the copper phone lines. Copper is incredibly conductive, obviously, second only to silver. Silver tarnishes, though, because it reacts with hydrogen sulfide in the air. I was actually reading last night about how you can use basic electrolysis with baking soda and aluminum foil to reverse the silver sulfide reaction and turn it back into solid silver. You just need a weak electrolyte solution and some boiling water... wait, what were you asking me? About being happy?
Have you ever had a period of time where you felt extremely happy, energetic, and impulsive that lasted for several days or more, without any significant breaks or returns to normal?

Yeah, without any breaks. It's been going on for about three months now, ever since my platform was selected for the Glendale showcase. It's just been this constant, high-voltage energy since then. 

Voltage, you know, is really just electrical potential difference. It's the pressure that pushes the electrons through the conductor. People always confuse voltage and current. Current is what actually kills you, the amperage. It only takes about 50 milliamps across the heart to cause ventricular fibrillation. That's why those old CRT monitors were so dangerous to work on if you didn't discharge the flyback transformer properly. Those things could hold thousands of volts even after being unplugged for days because they acted like massive capacitors. 

Capacitors are fascinating components. They store energy in an electrostatic field between two conductive plates separated by a dielectric insulator. In the early days, they called them Leyden jars, invented back in the 1700s. Benjamin Franklin used them in his famous kite experiment. He actually hooked multiple Leyden jars together in parallel to increase the total capacitance, and he called it a "battery" because it reminded him of a battery of artillery cannons firing together. It's funny how military terminology just bleeds into everything we do. Even the term "debugging" in software came from Grace Hopper finding an actual physical moth stuck in a relay of the Harvard Mark II electromechanical computer in 1947. She taped it into the logbook and wrote "First actual case of bug being found." 

I actually started keeping a physical logbook for my home network project, bound in real leather. Leather binding is a dying art. You have to use a bone folder to crease the signatures perfectly before you sew them onto the linen tapes... wait, what did you ask me? About how long I've felt like this?

{"intent": "Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the criteria for a manic episode", "question": "Have you ever had a period of time where you felt extremely happy, energetic, and impulsive that lasted for several days or more, and during that time, did you require less sleep than usual without feeling tired?""}

Sleep? I mean, I'm not really sure if I need less of it, honestly. I haven't really been paying attention to the clock because I'm just so locked in at night. The nighttime is really the only time you can get into a pure flow state without people constantly pinging you on Slack. 

Slack is actually an acronym, you know. It stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." It's crazy how it completely replaced email for internal comms. Email is so archaic anyway, it runs on the SMTP protocol from the early 80s. The original RFC for SMTP was written by Jon Postel. He was basically the god of the early internet, he managed the IANA all by himself for years. He actually used to keep track of all the IP address allocations in a simple paper notebook. Imagine that! The entire routing table of the early ARPANET just jotted down in a notebook. 

Notebooks are great, though. Like I was saying about the leather binding... paper itself is fascinating. The Chinese invented it during the Han dynasty, using mulberry bark and hemp. Hemp is incredibly versatile, you can make rope, textiles, paper, even bioplastics out of it. Henry Ford actually built a car prototype in 1941 that had plastic body panels made from hemp and soybeans. It was supposed to be lighter and safer than steel, but World War II happened and they just abandoned the project because they needed all the resources for the war effort... wait, what did you ask me? Did you ask about my Slack messages?

Happy and energetic? Yeah, absolutely. Most days lately I feel completely lit up and just... unstoppable. It’s like Glendale finally caught up with what I’ve been building all this time. But I will admit, I snap pretty hard when my wife or my coworkers try to slow me down with what they call "process." 

Process! Don't even get me started on process. At work, they are obsessed with Agile methodologies, and we use Jira to track every little thing. Jira is such a bloated piece of software now. Did you know it was originally built just for bug tracking, and the name actually comes from "Gojira", which is the Japanese name for Godzilla? They named it that because it was supposed to be a competitor to Bugzilla, which was this old Mozilla project back in the late 90s. 

The internet back then was so much more raw and decentralized. You had to dial in with those 56k modems, and that crazy screeching handshake sound you'd hear? That was actually the modems negotiating the connection speed and protocol. It's a process called "training", where they send test signals back and forth to measure the signal-to-noise ratio on the copper phone lines. Copper is incredibly conductive, obviously, second only to silver. Silver tarnishes, though, because it reacts with hydrogen sulfide in the air. I was actually reading last night about how you can use basic electrolysis with baking soda and aluminum foil to reverse the silver sulfide reaction and turn it back into solid silver. You just need a weak electrolyte solution and some boiling water... wait, what were you asking me? About being happy?

patient.answer:
Yeah, without any breaks. It's been going on for about three months now, ever since my platform was selected for the Glendale showcase. It's just been this constant, high-voltage energy since then. 

Voltage, you know, is really just electrical potential difference. It's the pressure that pushes the electrons through the conductor. People always confuse voltage and current. Current is what actually kills you, the amperage. It only takes about 50 milliamps across the heart to cause ventricular fibrillation. That's why those old CRT monitors were so dangerous to work on if you didn't discharge the flyback transformer properly. Those things could hold thousands of volts even after being unplugged for days because they acted like massive capacitors. 

Capacitors are fascinating components. They store energy in an electrostatic field between two conductive plates separated by a dielectric insulator. In the early days, they called them Leyden jars, invented back in the 1700s. Benjamin Franklin used them in his famous kite experiment. He actually hooked multiple Leyden jars together in parallel to increase the total capacitance, and he called it a "battery" because it reminded him of a battery of artillery cannons firing together. It's funny how military terminology just bleeds into everything we do. Even the term "debugging" in software came from Grace Hopper finding an actual physical moth stuck in a relay of the Harvard Mark II electromechanical computer in 1947. She taped it into the logbook and wrote "First actual case of bug being found." 

I actually started keeping a physical logbook for my home network project, bound in real leather. Leather binding is a dying art. You have to use a bone folder to crease the signatures perfectly before you sew them onto the linen tapes... wait, what did you ask me? About how long I've felt like this?

Slack is actually an acronym, you know. It stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." It's crazy how it completely replaced email for internal comms. Email is so archaic anyway, it runs on the SMTP protocol from the early 80s. The original RFC for SMTP was written by Jon Postel. He was basically the god of the early internet, he managed the IANA all by himself for years. He actually used to keep track of all the IP address allocations in a simple paper notebook. Imagine that! The entire routing table of the early ARPANET just jotted down in a notebook. 

Notebooks are great, though. Like I was saying about the leather binding... paper itself is fascinating. The Chinese invented it during the Han dynasty, using mulberry bark and hemp. Hemp is incredibly versatile, you can make rope, textiles, paper, even bioplastics out of it. Henry Ford actually built a car prototype in 1941 that had plastic body panels made from hemp and soybeans. It was supposed to be lighter and safer than steel, but World War II happened and they just abandoned the project because they needed all the resources for the war effort... wait, what did you ask me?
